subtopic: TABLING OF REPORTS OF ACTUARIAL VALUATIONS

speakeroldname: Hon. Waller L. Gordon (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: TABLING OF REPORTS OF ACTUARIAL VALUATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today I am tabling the reports of the quinquennial actuarial valuations required under sections 33 and 48 of the Public Service Superannuation Act.
The most important of these reports deals with the state of the superannuation account as of December 31, 1962 and shows that new deficiencies of $110,536,000 arose during the five year period ending on that day. The largest contributory factor was the deficiency arising from salary adjustments authorized in 1960 and again in 1962 for various classes of contributors. Subsequently the salary increases authorized in July, 1963 with effect from October 1, 1962 added another $22 million to this deficiency.
In accordance with the policy outlined in this house on March 6 of this year authority will be sought from parliament later in this fiscal year to write off to net debt the initial deficiency of $110,536,000 plus interest, and to charge the deficiencies arising from pay increases authorized during the fiscal years 1963-64 and 1964-65 against expenditures over a five year period commencing with this fiscal year. Thus one fifth of the deficit of $22 million plus interest and one fifth of the deficiencies arising from subsequent similar salary increases will be charged to expenditure during the fiscal year 1964-65.
The other two reports which I have tabled related to the death benefit accounts established under part II of the act. These reports show that a satisfactory contingency reserve is being built up.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Prime Minister. Is he now in a position to indicate to the house the terms of the reply he sent on Tuesday to those who were concerned about increases in pensions of retired civil servants, and were those terms favourable?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: SUPERANNUATED FEDERAL EMPLOYEES- REQUEST FOR INCREASED PENSIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, replies have gone to the representatives of the federal superannuates national association, to the civil service federation of Canada and to the civil service association of Canada. These replies have now been received by them, so I think it is appropriate for me to announce in the house that the government has come to the conclusion- and this was embodied in the replies-after reviewing the principles involved and the facts cited, that any steps it should propose to parliament to alleviate difficulties faced by retired persons should be general in character and not confined to former employees of the government of Canada.


The government believe, in the light of general action already taken and proposed to benefit all retired people in Canada-I am referring here, of course, among other things, to the old age security pension-that it would be unfair to the great majority of retired Canadians who have not worked for the government to make special provisions to benefit only former employees of the government of Canada. To do so would constitute, in a sense, a form of discrimination against the majority of other retired Canadians who cannot expect such treatment from the government as such, or generally from their former employers.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Tuesday, November 10, consideration in committee of Bill No. C-72, to provide for the establishment of electoral boundaries commissions to report upon the readjustment of the representation of the provinces in the House of Commons and to provide for the readjustment of such representation in accordance therewith-Mr. Pickersgill (for Mr. Pearson)-Mr. Lamoureux in the chair.
On clause 6-Appointment of chairman.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, on Tuesday the minister discussed clause 6, this clause having been set aside while the other clauses of the bill were discussed. On that occasion
Electoral Boundaries Commissions the minister put two propositions to the committee regarding a change to clause 6. Without going into detail my suggestion at that time, which was accepted by the minister- and I thank him for that-was that the debate be adjourned and the bill discussed again today so that in the interim we could discuss these two proposed changes to clause 6.
We have now had a discussion Mr. Chairman, and have come to a conclusion. It was the feeling of the group in this party who met that as far as we were concerned, although we preferred the terms and conditions of the bill as originally drawn and presented by the minister, in order to compromise and come to some sort of settlement so we could get this legislation through the house we should give serious thought and consideration to accepting one of the changes suggested by the minister.
One of the proposals was that two members of the commission be appointed by the Speaker of the House of Commons. We believe this proposal has some merit, although as I say we would prefer to accept the original bill as drawn by the government and presented to parliament. Nevertheless sometimes consideration must be given to other people's viewpoints, and we have given such consideration to that suggestion.
In arriving at that conclusion I should like to summarize what has been our position in the past with reference to this redistribution bill. We received some criticism to the effect that there was delay on our part with reference to the passage of this particular piece of legislation. We felt that as a matter of principle the commission should be made up of personnel appointed by the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition who would sit with the commissioner. It was then that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre moved his amendment, which was known-I think I can say this without slighting the hon. member-as the Knowles amendment. It was at that stage that we reached a deadlock on the bill.
Therefore, what was our position? First of all, our party's position was that we should have one commission for all Canada; that if there were to be ten commissions the bill should have been left as it was so the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition each in turn would appoint one member of the commissions. At that time the minister had this to say, and it might be well to review it because he did leave the gate open. As reported at page 741 of Hansard for March 10, 1964 he said:
10000	HOUSE OF
Electoral Boundaries Commissions
After various other possibilities were considered the government finally agreed to put in the bill the suggestion that the chief justice of the province should nominate the chairman from a member of his court; that the leader of the government, the Prime Minister, should nominate one of the members of the commission; and that the Leader of the Opposition, who is an officer of parliament, should nominate the other. I say unreservedly that I have every confidence that no matter who occupies those offices, any person who becomes leader of the opposition in the parliament of our country or prime minister in the parliament of our country would take this responsibility seriously and make the kind of nominations that all of us would feel were appropriate under the circumstances. I do not hesitate to say that with respect to this provision or with respect to any other method which commends itself to the house or to a majority of the house and which seems likely to produce as fair and effective a result, the government will be quite prepared in committee to consider on its merits any amendments to this procedure.
To be fair to the minister, he did leave the door open at that time, and it was left open both for the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and any other member of this committee. At that time the amendment was moved.
Now, Mr. Chairman, we objected to the amendment on similar grounds to those outlined by the minister on Tuesday, namely that one person would be appointing three people. We also objected to it on the ground that those people were to be appointed from a certain group of people in a certain category. We contended that in some respects that could lead to discrimination. In fact it might mean that people with practical experience and knowledge of politics and who would then be referred to as politicians might be discriminated against.
Therefore we as a group feel that the solution to this problem is to accept one of the propositions which have been put forward by the minister, so we can get the bill approved by this house and the commissioners can get on with the job. The proposition is that the Speaker appoint two of the members of the commission. Let us take a look at this for a moment. The Speaker, as the minister said on Tuesday, is elected by the members of the House of Commons. He sits in a judicial capacity in the House of Commons. Certainly my experience has been-and there are many here who are my seniors-that the Speaker has always exercised his position judiciously, as I am sure would any Speaker given that responsibility by the house. Certainly I know we would have every confidence that the present Speaker would exercise his powers judiciously in this regard.


Therefore, after some consideration and serious thought, we would entertain a change to clause 6 of the bill so the two other members of the commission would be appointed by the Speaker. No doubt the Speaker would consult with the leader of the government and the Leader of the Opposition and the leaders of the other parties in making his choice. But I repeat that we feel his choice will a judicious one having regard to the fact that we want to set up a commission which is as close to purity as we can get it so the question of redistribution is taken out of the field of politics.
This position we have taken is, of course, predicated on the fact that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre will withdraw his amendment. In order to get this bill through now and let the commissioners get on with the job of redistribution, which is a very big job, I trust the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre will recognize that we have compromised our previous stand. We repeat that we would rather have had the bill in its original form. We dislike the bill as it would be amended by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, and we are suggesting some compromise. It is not exactly what we would like, but it is the best we can do today in order to reach a compromise.
When I say a compromise, it is really a settlement. I looked up the meaning of the word "compromise", and the best definition I could find in the Oxford dictionary was that it means to meet half way or to reach a settlement. I think this is the best settlement of the dilemma in which we have been.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre seems to have been making other statements outside this house since this was discussed on Tuesday, and one can never be too sure of the position he might take. However, I sincerely trust that because of the compromise we are making he will also compromise his position. I should like to congratulate the minister for the compromise he has adopted. Since we have reached consideration of the clause of this bill having to do with these appointments, I hope the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre will realize that the only solution to be found to the problem lies in a withdrawal of his amendment.
Mr. Chairman, I should like very much to hear from the minister and from the member for Winnipeg North Centre as to what they think about the position we are adopting.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Bow River has pointed out that the members of this house have had 48 hours to consider the proposals which were placed before the house on Tuesday afternoon. The hon. member has said that the members of his group have considered those proposals. The same is true of us in this party. We have looked at both proposals offered by the Minister of Transport in the light of what we believe to be the desire of parliament regarding redistribution.
I shall spell out the reasons for our position, but I might as well not keep the member for Bow River or anyone else in suspense. We do not feel disposed to withdraw our amendment for the purpose of agreeing to either of the amendments proposed by the Minister of Transport. Perhaps it is not necessary to discuss, in more than a sentence or two, the second proposal made by the minister, because apparently the Progressive Conservatives are not interested in it either. May I say that the second proposal strikes us as being worse than the first one.
Mr. Chairman, the second proposal was that each individual provincial commission consist of four people with votes and three people with eyes and voices but without votes. These other three were to be appointed, one each by the leaders of the three other parties in the House of Commons. We feel that an arrangement of that kind would really turn this so-called impartial redistribution into a political dogfight, and if that proposal were put forward we would oppose it very strongly. However, it is not even being considered by the Progressive Conservatives, so we do not have to deal with it further.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: We thought it would be unfair to you.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
We do not think it would be unfair to us, we think it would be unfair to the people of Canada, and we think it would be adverse to the principle we have already agreed to in this house.
We now come to the other proposal the Minister of Transport has made, which the hon. member for Bow River says his party is prepared to accept, namely that in the legislation the Speaker of the House of Commons be asked to name the other two members of each of the ten provincial commissions. The first comment I want to make is to the effect that I find the bit of logic which we have been handed rather difficult to understand.
Electoral Boundaries Commissions
The Minister of Transport used an expression the other day which the hon. member for Bow River has just repeated. Maybe they have consulted during the last 48 hours. At any rate, this is what the Minister of Transport said on Tuesday, as recorded at page 9954 of Hansard. I note the way Hansard is building up. It probably has reached 10,000 pages by now for the first time in Canadian history. At any rate this is what the minister said:
It is true that there were limitations on the kind of persons who could he appointed, but notwithstanding that fact, that is perhaps rather a concentration of power in the hands of one man-
That was in reference to the chief justice, under the terms of my amendment, appointing three persons. That statement was made by the Minister of Transport and has now been made by the hon. member for Bow River. They have said it would be rather a concentration of power in the hands of one man to ask one man to make three appointments, but now the proposal is that we ask one man to make 20 appointments. The suggestion is that we ask the Speaker to appoint two members to each of the ten provincial commissions. Please tell me how the power to appoint three members is a concentration of power in the hands of one man and that you get away from that by giving to one man the power to appoint 20 persons.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I wonder whether the hon. member would permit a question. Would he not consider in fairness that each of these commissions has jurisdiction over matters in its own province? There are ten separate commissions to be set up, one for each province, which will have jurisdiction in reference to that province. In other words the commission set up for the province of Ontario will not be governing in the jurisdiction of the province of Alberta. Is that not fair?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
That is a typical attempt on the part of the hon. member for Bow River to answer a point, and is a complete non sequitur if ever there was one. Of course there are ten separate provincial commissions. What we are talking about is the basis of the argument made against our proposal, which was that the power of appointment, with which we are dealing in our consideration of clause 6, as suggested by our amendment, was being concentrated because one man was being given the power to appoint three people. Now the proposal is that one man be given the power to appoint 20 people. I suggest that that is logic in reverse.

Electoral Boundaries Commissions

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: It sounds pretty illogical to me.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: It certainly is, and I am glad I have convinced my hon. friend.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: I was referring to your argument.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: An argument in this chamber during a debate of this kind is much like the argument about motherhood. No one criticizes motherhood. We have the name of Mr. Speaker put before us, and all our respect for the Chair and our confidence in the impartiality of the Speaker is brought into play. When I think of the number of times the hon. member for Bow River has not even accepted the judgment of Mr. Speaker, as he did today when his question was ruled out of order, it becomes rather strange that the hon. member feels the Speaker is such an impartial person he could make these appointments across the country.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order. I did not challenge the Speaker's ruling during the question period today just before orders of the day were called. The minister did not answer the question and according to the rules laid down by the hon. member, who has been so proud of the changes, I rose and said that I should like to have it debated at ten o'clock. That is not a challenge of a judicial decision of His Honour the Speaker, and certainly represents no disrespect for him. I think the hon. member should withdraw his remark, and if he has a sound argument let us get on with it.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
That is non sequitur No. 2, Mr. Chairman. Let us get back to the issue.
The argument is put forward that somehow or other by asking Mr. Speaker to make these appointments we would take this whole matter out of politics. Does any Speaker of the House of Commons know the personalities and situations of each of the ten provinces of this country? Is there any person who is likely to occupy the chair of this house who is in a position on his own to make these appointments? The answer is obviously in the negative. If this job is entrusted to the Speaker he is going to have to obtain advice and consult someone. I think the cat was let out of the bag by the hon. member for Bow River when he agreed to that suggestion and said his party understood that if this amendment were accepted the Speaker would consult the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition and then, 

out of the kindness of his heart, he said the Speaker would probably consult the leaders of the other parties.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: I put them all in the same category.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, my hon.
friend and I are in agreement in that regard, but what he does not seem to realize is that by doing so we are keeping redistribution as a partisan and political affair. The whole purpose of the legislation before us-and the Minister of Transport said this was the only aspect of it on which the government would stand or fall-is that we are going to put redistribution beyond parliament, we are going to put it in the hands of an impartial commission, we are going to have these boundaries drawn objectively by people outside the parliamentary arena. But under the terms of the proposed amendment we are going to have two of the appointees to each of these commissions given their positions by Mr. Speaker on the basis of an understanding, stated in the House of Commons, that he will have consulted the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition and the leaders of the other parties. In other words we are making it quite clear that what we are going to get is appointments that are political in one sense or the other. Either they are political in that they are proposed by political persons, or they are political in the sense that they do not displease the political leaders of the various parties in the House of Commons.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: I wonder whether the hon. gentleman would permit me to ask him a question. Does he know how these appointments are made in the United Kingdom?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: I had hoped that in this house we were going to move a step ahead.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: Does he know?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: Yes. In the United Kingdom they are made by order in council.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: No, they are not.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
If my hon. friend knows something about this that I do not know I would be glad if he would so advise me, but my general understanding of the practice in the United Kingdom is that they have not gone as far in the direction of impartiality as it was proposed to go in the bill brought in by the government here, and we welcomed the attempt of the government, supported by all parties in the house, really to go in for a

non-political, impartial redistribution of the seats in the House of Commons.
I suggest that when you have people appointed in this way you are not going to achieve the high ideal that we started out with when the bill was introduced. I also submit that this puts a terrific load on Mr. Speaker himself. He has his hands full administering the staff and the affairs of the House of Commons. He has a full time job just occupying the chair and retaining that impartiality that goes with the occupancy of the chair in the House of Commons. To impose upon him now this very highly political chore of naming these people to these various commissions across the country is, I submit, unfair to him and out of line with the basic principles of this legislation.
The hon. member for Bow River quite properly has drawn attention to the willingness of his party to compromise, and I do not detract from that by one iota. For a long time his party seemed unwilling to agree to anything except clause 6 in its original form. He now says they are prepared to agree to clause 6 in the terms proposed by the Minister of Transport in one of the amendments. That is a change of position. If the Liberals had changed like that the Tories would call it a retreat but I will not do that.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: On a question of privilege, Mr. Chairman, I know the hon. gentleman always wants to be fair. The Liberals have never taken a position on this bill except on one point, as the hon. gentleman fairly said before. We consider that every member should be guided by his own conscience in this matter, which is the equal responsibility of every member of this parliament. I hope the hon. gentleman will take my words sincerely and not ascribe positions that I have taken to anybody but myself.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
I have no quarrel with what the Minister of Transport has just said. In fact I want to endorse what he has said, to the effect that the only point in this whole matter that the government has regarded as sacred, if you will, or that the government has regarded as a point on which it would stand or fall, is on the basic proposition of redistribution being taken out of parliament and given to an independent body. My contention is that we are denying that basic principle if we set up that body on terms under which its independence is not as clear as it really could be.
Electoral Boundaries Commissions
I started to say that I recognize the element of compromise that has been indicated on the part of the official opposition, and I do not want members to think our position is an immovable one and that we insist on the terms of my amendment to clause 6 and nothing else. We too are prepared to negotiate, to find some middle ground if it is at all possible to do so. I was wondering whether over the 48 hour interval there might be some attempt at negotiation of the point, but there was none, at least so far as my experience is concerned in the last two days.
But I want to say to the government and the official opposition as well that if the objection to my amendment-and after all it is my amendment we are still officially discussing-is that it places this power of appointment in the hands of the chief justice of the province, which some people do not like, we would have no objection to changing the situs of that power of appointment. We would have no objection to substituting the Speaker for the chief justice in so far as making these appointments is concerned, but we do feel that the kind of advice, the guide lines, the directions that are contained in my amendment should be given to the Speaker as well.
We would suggest that either one of two things be tried as a means of arriving at a consensus among all five parties in the house. After all, the government is really in no better position to win the support of one party and lose the support of two or three others than it would have been if it had stayed where it was. I suggest that as a basis for arriving at a consensus among all five parties either one of two things might be done.

We had such fine support from the hon. member for Cariboo when this matter was up before, but apparently he has got tired of it. I suggest either one of two things, either that my amendment be amended by substituting the Speaker for the chief justice but leaving in the amendment the categories from which the Speaker would make the choices, or that the government should indicate that it will add words to its amendment so far as the power of appointment by the Speaker is concerned. The government's amendment could read that these appointments be made by Mr. Speaker provided, however, that the appointments or at least one of them be made from a certain class or category of persons.

Electoral Boundaries Commissions
As an offer to compromise, as an offer to find some basis on which we might all agree, I suggest that provision should be made in the proposal, whichever way it comes about, whether by way of amendment to my amendment or amendment to the government's amendment, for our proposal that one of these appointees, whether he is named by the chief justice or by the Speaker, should be the chief electoral officer of the province, the surveyor general, the recorder of vital statistics or a person of that kind.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I want to make it clear that we are prepared to withdraw our amendment if an alternative is put forward that is acceptable to all of us and in keeping with the basic principle of the bill, but if no such acceptable alternative is brought forward we would not, of course, be willing to withdraw our amendment. We feel it is in keeping with the basic principle of the bill itself, and that if the house does not want our amendment it will have to vote it down rather than expecting us to withdraw it.

Mr. Chairman, taking into consideration the two alternative proposals by the Minister of Transport with regard to the previously moved amendment to clause 6, it becomes obvious that in trying to find perfection in the selection of the commissions we become involved immediately in different interpretations of perfection.
Now, Mr. Chairman, in looking over the two alternative proposals it seems to me that the one that returns to the appointment of some members of the commission by the leader of the government in the house and the Leader of the Opposition in the House of Commons is not essentially different from clause 6 in the original bill. I should say that we were not particularly happy with the idea of trying to set up what might be called a non-partisan redistribution commission and then turning around and allowing the leaders of the two major political parties in the country to appoint 50 per cent of the membership of these commissions. I think therefore, so far as we are concerned, we can almost disregard that particular proposal.
We come, then, to the second proposal that has been suggested. We think there is some merit in having the Speaker of this chamber appoint at least some of the members of these redistribution commissions. Certainly it is true, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has said, that the Speaker will be appointing 20 commissioners across the country. He will also, it is expected, seek advice

from someone, but we do not disagree with that at all. What is more, we think he may even seek advice from some of the political parties in the country. There seems to have been an attempt to downgrade the advice that can be received from political organizations in the country in so far as redistribution is concerned. I suppose it is fair to say that each political party will certainly have to take into consideration its own interests in redistribution. At the same time, this would be offset by other parties making their representations as well.
I do not subscribe to this theory, if you want to call it such, that the advice that can come to these commissions from political parties would be all bad. I think even the practice we have had in the past, that has been deplored in some cases, has not been that bad. Certainly political organizations are keenly interested, and I might say some of the executive officers of the political organizations within a constituency probably have a better knowledge of some of the problems of organizing or setting up constituencies in the light of such considerations as natural boundaries, community of interest and so on, than any other groups in the country.
Overriding the consideration of finding a perfect formula for nominating the members of this commission, Mr. Chairman, is the fact that redistribution is long overdue. I believe perhaps the second alternative proposal is as close to perfection as we can reach at this time. I want to say this, too, whether we accept the original draft of clause 6 in Bill No. C-72 or the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre or either of the two alternatives that have been presented to us within the last 48 hours. Overriding all that is the fact that we need to have redistribution. If we do not reach some kind of agreement soon we are going to have another election based on the 1951 census. In my opinion this would be a far greater disservice to the electorate in Canada than anything that could come about from any one of the four proposals that are before us. I feel that the limit imposed by clause 13, for example, whether it is 20 per cent, 25 per cent or even 33J per cent, will be such that there will not be a great deal of discretion left to the commissioners in so far as the size of a constituency is concerned. Certainly there will be some discretion in the minor adjustment of borders, but at least the limit imposed by clause 13 does remove a great deal of the dis-

cretionary power redistribution commissions have had in the past.
Speaking directly to the change from the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre to the new proposals, I would say that I do not accept the contention that the president or a similar officer or member of the faculty of a university would be any less partisan politically than the Speaker of this house. As a matter of fact I believe the Speaker would be considerably less partisan, if I may put it that way, than most of the members of these faculties. I feel that the question before us, therefore, at least the paramount question before us, is to accept one or the other of these four proposals and get on with setting up the redistribution commission so that it can be done, rather than squabbling over what might be called the minor details in seeking perfection.
An important idea, by the way, advanced by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre was that the chief electoral officer of a province or perhaps the surveyor general of a province should be a member of the commission. There are a number of reasons for that, I think. First of all, for example, the chief electoral officer of a province of necessity would be very familiar with the topography, community of interests and so on because he has been involved in these things within the provincial jurisdiction. He would be a very useful member on the commission simply because of his knowledge of the province, regardless of what his politics might be. We would hope, of course, that he did not have any partisan political tendency that would guide his thinking.
The other reason that the chief electoral officer of the province would be a useful member of the commission is that he could probably give some guidance to the commission in so far as making the boundaries of a number of provincial constituencies coterminus with the boundaries of federal constituencies. This is a matter that has some merit because I know that, particularly in the first election following redistribution, there is a great deal of confusion along the boundaries of both federal and provincial constituencies. People get used to going to certain polling places. They get used to dealing with the old set-up, if you want to call it that, and it is a little difficult to educate them or to inform the electorate of the constituencies about the many changes that may have been made.
I am not going to speak any longer, Mr. Chairman. I think we would prefer to accept
Electoral Boundaries Commissions the alternative proposal which gives the Speaker of this house the power to name two of the members on the ten commissions. If anything could be done to give some guidance to the Speaker, along the lines that one of the men to be appointed should possibly be the chief electoral officer or the surveyor general of a province, that might be useful. But we are not prepared to hold up the adoption of clause 6, because we think redistribution, based on a more recent census than that of 1951, is a more important consideration than these minor details.

But not on the same commission, as the hon. member for Bow River pointed out. There will be only two persons on each commission appointed by one appointor, and two others appointed in a different manner. That is certainly less concentration of power than to have three appointed by one person on each separate commission.
As for the tremendous difficulties and burden this will impose upon the Speaker, I think he can well bear them, considering the other burdens we place on him every day. I am totally unimpressed with that argument. Like the hon. member for Medicine Hat I believe the most important thing is to carry out our constitutional responsibility to make sure there is a redistribution which, as we all know, is long overdue. That is the overriding consideration.
This other rather complicated scheme I put forward also has a precedent in New Zealand, and I think it would not result in an unsatisfactory, unfair or partisan redistribution. I do not think any of them would, but of all four the one I like best is the one giving these appointments to the Speaker. I believe he will seek to appoint, wherever they are available-and this is all the hon. member's amendment would do-officers like the chief electoral officer of a province and the surveyor general of a province, someone who is technically competent; but we cannot force him to do so, and we cannot force these people to act. That is the original difficulty we had in this matter.
Therefore I am not much in favour of trying to put this condition into the amendment

itself; but when the hon. member's amendment is disposed of and if the house does not accept it-I guess it will not-then if he wants to move a subamendment he can test the committee on this point. That is his right, and I think that would be the proper way to do it. Personally I feel that if we are going to give this task to His Honour the Speaker, we should give it to him, period. We should not seek to give it to him and then say, "We are just a little dubious about this and we think we ought to tell you how to do it."

speechtext: Has the minister forgotten the arguments he used in favour of my amendment when, if we were to give the job to the chief justices, he argued that we should give them guide lines?

Exactly; but I would remind the hon. gentleman that the chief justice of a province is not an officer of the parliament of Canada. He is not under our jurisdiction, and if there are any flagrant abuses of this power by His Honour the Speaker we have a remedy in our rules. It has been used only once or twice in our history, and I hope it will never be used for a long time again.
I am totally unimpressed with the suggestion that this would impose a terrible burden on the Speaker, or that there would be any difficulty, or that in any advice the Speaker should choose to take there would be any more suggestion of partisanship than in any other method of appointment which might possibly be devised. That is why I asked the hon. gentleman if he knew how appointments are made in the United Kingdom.
It might be useful to refresh hon. members' memories on that point. There are four commissions in the United Kingdom, one each for England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland, and the chairman of all four commissions is the Speaker of the House of Commons. I think it is true that his chairmanship is perhaps rather perfunctory but he has a voice and I suppose, being the chairman, he has the largest voice of all if he chooses to exercise it. The deputy chairman is a judge of the high court appointed by the lord chancellor.
There are two other members in the English commission, one appointed by the home secretary and the other by the minister of housing and local government. They are not even appointed by order in council; they are appointed by ministers. I do not think anyone in this house would want to trust ministers to make such appointments and at no time

have I suggested that this be done, but that is what is done in England and there has never been any real suggestion I know of that the English commission was not as nonpartisan as anything one could reasonably get. In Scotland the two ministerial appointments-there is a judge who is the deputy chairman-are made by the Secretary of Scotland. The situation is analogous for the other two commissions, and I think it would be wasting the time of the committee to go beyond that.
What we would be doing here, if we did not accept the hon. gentleman's amendment and instead accepted the one which I am now quite satisfied I would be justified in moving if the hon. gentleman's amendment is defeated, would be saying that the chairman of each commission shall be appointed by the chief justice of the province and, if there is any default, by the Chief Justice of Canada; that two other appointments apart from the representation commissioner would be made by the Speaker. We will be saying that we have enough confidence in whoever may be the Speaker of the House of Commons to feel that he will appoint the kind of people that it is the whole purpose of the legislation to have appointed; that is to say, persons who will be independent and objective in their judgment.
I have always thought, as I confessed on Tuesday, that this would be the best method, if it was acceptable to the house. The only fear I ever had about proposing it was that we might have a serious division in the house about it, which I would regret. But I do not think there was anything said by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that would lead one to hesitate to make this motion and to take the sense of the house about it. The kind of objections he made were not the kind of objections which reflected in any way at all upon the Speaker or upon the office of Speaker, and I am sure he did not intend to make any such reflection.

I just wish to say that I think we are moving along and are making progress, which is something the people of Canada are looking forward to. Mr. Chairman, I think the intention of the hon. member for Medicine Hat, echoed by the Minister of Transport and the hon. member for Cariboo, that an election based upon the 1951 census would be most unfair and injurious to the electorate carries with it, as they stated, the implication that we should therefore give passage to whatever measure might be presented to us, if it is presented in a reasonable way and if the arguments in favour of it appear on the surface to be reasonable. I think this is a somewhat misleading and somewhat false position to take.
It is correct that we are long overdue in carrying out the responsibilities that devolve upon parliament with regard to the question of redistribution following the decennial census, but I believe we should not let that consideration override the possibility that any bill which is before us is likely to be wrecked, adulterated or watered down from the original principle. I think this is likely to take place here.
Generally, Mr. Chairman, I am sure there is agreement that we want (1) to have a redistribution system as soon as possible in order that redistribution can take place, and (2) we want that system to be non-political. These two principles are correct, but they should not blind us to some of the other features which might be bad in attempting to put them into effect. I believe this might be the case here, with these compromise proposals that are being presented and argued. It is my understanding that there was a large degree of the spirit of co-operation among all the parties in this chamber up until Tuesday of this week, when the Minister of Transport placed the two alternate proposals on Hansard, but that since that time-I have consulted with the people in the New Democratic party who participate in these all-party meetings-there has not been any sort of discussion or consultation as has usually been the case in matters such as this. At least there has been no sort of consultation or discussion to which my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre was invited or in which he participated. I am not objecting to that in any way, and I

am sure he is not objecting either, but it does seem passing strange that all of a sudden there is agreement from those who previously raised the most stringent objections to the manner of proceeding as proposed in the bill introduced by the government.
I assume that what has taken place-I am not objecting to this, of course-is that there has been some behind the scenes consultation between the government and the official opposition in an attempt to reach a meeting of minds on what previously had been an impasse. As I say, I do not object to that, but if it did occur I think the fact should be placed on record so that the house and the general public will know that such arrangement did exist and that the Minister of Transport is not completely taken by surprise at the position of the official opposition. In fact I think he let the cat out of the bag when he virtually anticipated what the vote of this committee might be on the amendment before us if and when it did take place, which indicates that there was this prior consultation in an attempt to reach a meeting of minds. In fact, I would put the suggestion forward that such a meeting did take place, and in the absence of any denial of my suggestion I think we can accept as a fact that there was a behind the scenes meeting on the proposals now put before us.

Mr. Chairman, the highly flattering remarks of the minister have com-completely disarmed me. However, it is an undeniable fact, and should be obvious to anyone, that in its original form subclause 2 of clause 6 proposes that the two members of the commissions, other than the chairman and representation commissioner, would be appointed, one by the leader of the government in the House of Commons and one by the leader of the opposition in the House of Commons. When the minister now says that he never at any time intended anything other than that these appointments would be nonpolitical and non-partisan, I again say rubbish. The minister did say that which I have indicated, and that is what is said in the bill now before us. What could be more clear than that one of the two members of the commission, other than the chairman, shall be appointed by the leader of the government and one by the leader of the opposition? That is what the bill says, and if the minister is trying to suggest that that does not imply, or perhaps even more than imply, a desire for

Mr. Chairman, we know from past practice that leaders of governments in the House of Commons engage in politics and partisanships whenever there is an occasion to do so. I am not so naive that I could believe the Minister of Transport when he says that no prime minister is going to make political appointments if the occasion to do so arose. I believe that he might be enticed into doing that sort of thing.
The fact of the matter is that the original presentation of this bill, which was in the name of the Prime Minister, admittedly, and not in the name of the Minister of Transport, provided for appointments to be made by the prime minister and the leader of the opposition. Perhaps if the bill had been under the sponsorship of the Minister of Transport we would now have a completely different proposal without this obvious attempt at partisanship.
Regardless of how often the Minister of Transport says that he did not mean there should be partisanship, or that he does not believe in that sort of thing, the proposal made by the Minister of Transport, in respect of the mechanism by which one of these commissioners would be appointed, would lead us in the direction again of political partisanship in the selection of the members of these commissions, through influence brought to bear on whomever happened to occupy the position of Mr. Speaker. I do not say that in a derogatory way, but so long as the office of Mr. Speaker is a political office, and not a permanent non-partisan one, which I am sure we would all like to see, this possibility would remain.
My second point in argument against the proposal of the Minister of Transport is that it is regrettable that Mr. Speaker should be dragged into the political activities of this nation even more than he has been dragged in at the moment. Every government in recent times has expressed the feeling, shared I think by all members of this house, or at least of this party, that Mr. Speaker should be a non-partisan individual. I think we are
Electoral Boundaries Commissions all in favour of the sort of semi-colonial attitude, that whatever is done in the United Kingdom should be done here, namely that we should have a Speaker who in fact occupies an honoured position for a long period of time, and that his office should be removed from political activity not only on a day to day basis but as well during political campaigning. The fact of the matter is that this is not the case. I do not know how far away the time is, and perhaps the sooner the better, but Mr. Macnaughton, our present Speaker, will be running as a candidate in his own constituency. Presumably there will be, as there has been in the past, candidates of other political parties running against him. As has happened to previous Speakers, he will find himself embroiled in political controversy, perhaps emanating from the bill we are considering at this time. Perhaps his riding will be redistributed; such has happened in the past. In fact I have heard the Leader of the Opposition say that the terrible Liberals have wiped his seat out from under him time after time.

When I used the word "seat" I knew what I was referring to, but whether or not the hon. member for Bow River did is another question. The Speaker will be involved and embroiled in political activity and controversy in a partisan way, and I assume he will still be a Liberal candidate in the next election. What we say we want to have happen is to have the Speaker set apart from political partisanship. We do not even like the fact that at election time he has to run under a party label, with candidates of the other parties running against the Speaker, because we want to preserve his position on a non-political and non-partisan basis in order to guarantee, if it needs to be guaranteed, that the rules of the house will be enforced in an impartial and non-political way.
But instead of moving in the direction of placing Mr. Speaker in an even more nonpartisan position because of the office he holds it is now proposed that we should move in the direction of bringing him into politics by dragging him into consultation with political leaders in order to select the members of the redistribution commission which we want to be non-political. I think this is regrettable.
It is for these reasons that I say we should not rush madly into endorsing one or other of the proposals which are before us at least

Electoral Boundaries Commissions by way of suggestion, if not in a formal way. We should not do so merely because we happen to have a strong desire to pass a redistribution bill in order that redistribution may be made on the basis of the 1961 census before the next election takes place. Incidentally, while we are on the subject of elections, we could very well have an election on our hands within the next few months. Everyone tells me this is quite possible and that it is probable that such an election would be conducted on the basis of the 1951 rather than the 1961 census. I am sure the minister will know more about that than I do because of his closer consultation with individuals in the office of the chief electoral officer, as well as his knowledge of other matters. Be that as it may, for the reasons I have outlined I submit we do not want to be seduced into endorsing either of the proposals now before us merely because there is a desire to hurry and pass the bill. Hurrying to get the bill through is commendable in itself, but in trying to do so we must not destroy the main principle, the establishment of redistribution commissions on a non-political and non-partisan basis.
In my opinion the proposal of the Minister of Transport that Mr. Speaker should make these appointments makes the bill even worse than it was in its original form. In its original form political partisanship was at least out in the open where everyone could see it and we could expect certain things to take place. Now it will be hidden behind the scenes. In addition, we are attempting to drag Mr. Speaker into the political arena and partisan activities to a far greater extent than he is at the moment, and in the process we are likely to degrade even further the office of Speaker, when what we want to do is to elevate it.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre made some alternative suggestions to the proposal of the Minister of Transport. I submit they should be looked at very carefully. I do not think we should rush helter-skelter into picking one or other of the amendments which have been suggested. In another 20 or 25 minutes we will reach private members' hour starting at five o'clock, which is followed by the supper recess. I suggest it should be possible during this interval for the leaders of the parties or their spokesmen to get together and consult on this matter and see whether or not they cannot work out some generally acceptable compromise amendment. In the light of the variety of things that have been said I submit that is a far better way to approach the matter than to follow the


suggestion of the Minister of Transport that we should have a vote right away on the amendment which has been before the committee for some months, when he will then proceed to move another amendment which just came to our attention a couple of days ago and about which, as the Minister of Transport has said, there has been no consultation with anybody.
I think we should put the consultative process to work, provide an opportunity for the various parties to consult and maybe by eight o'clock they will be able to arrive at a workable, worth-while amendment. If there is unanimity with regard to such an amendment, the possibility of political partisanship will be even further removed. I think this is the principal objective we all want to achieve, the carrying out of redistribution on a strictly non-political basis because we have had too much of political interference in the past.

search officer, to compel the premature, public disclosure of documents which are incomplete in themselves and which do not represent the standard of scholarship and of final preparation of material which is the mark of integrity of the civil service.
What the hon. member seeks to secure by this resolution is the publication of a series of premature, early drafts of reports which are incomplete, likely to be misinterpreted and which would do no service to Canadian unity. I do not believe it would serve the house or Canada to have this kind of material placed before the house in the form in which the hon. member who moved the motion presumably intends. I know there have been references to this matter in the press. There was a reference some weeks ago in Le Devoir, a front page story of a study in the Department of Finance, which presumed to make certain findings. We have now seen the final results as a result of screening, editing and polishing; and I use "polishing" in the sense of correcting inaccuracies or the exploring of areas of the subject matter which call for more careful attention. The results of that study have been filed and placed before this house. What can be the purpose of the mover of this motion in proceeding with it, in the face of the answers that were given by the Department of Finance to questions of an exactly similar nature posed by the hon. member for Three Rivers?
I think all members of this house should ponder the fundamental principle involved here. Are they going to, if they vote for such a motion-which I hope they will not- establish the principle that there should be no confidentiality of early drafts, of early reports of research officers in different branches of government? It would destroy scholarship within the research divisions of those men and women who serve this country and serve it well, who serve it with distinction and who are recognized in their professional capacity, if they did not have the right to work at their material, produce preliminary drafts, rework the preliminary drafts and stay with this material until they came to the conclusions and the results which they felt in their conscience and integrity they were prepared to support.
A parallel in regard to any form of research can readily be brought to mind. Someone doing laboratory research, who does experiments and makes certain initial findings which suggest certain hypotheses, does not publish these results right away. He tests them; he sets them up against repeated observation

Motions for Papers
and experiment before the results are placed, as contributions to knowledge, in the public record. The acceptance of a motion of this nature would destroy the integrity of research operations in the federal civil service and would have very serious repercussions in terms of morale, in terms of the operations of government departments and in terms of the government itself of this country. I know that the mover of the motion thinks he can gain certain advantage by consistently pursuing a question which has been the subject of a great deal of ill informed speculation. There is the question in terms of federal expenditures. The hon. member who questioned the Minister of Finance the other day raised the matter of interest on the national debt. The question was asked, how was this distributed by provinces, and the assumption was that this would be done on a per capita basis. The mover of the motion then asked, "What would happen in the case of payments, in regard to the federal debt, of persons who reside outside Canada? What allowances are made?" Again this illustrates the very difficult and involved technical preparations that must be part of any such study, not only on the expenditures side but on the revenue side.
The Minister of Finance indicated, in response to questions asked in the early stages of debate on this motion, that revenues which are raised in any particular part of the country cannot be ascribed at first glance simply to the place from which they are reported. Sales taxes paid by a manufacturing concern are in fact paid in many different parts of the country; customs duties levied at one port cannot be properly ascribed to any one province without a careful examination of the nature of the goods on which duty has been paid.
The problem of distribution involves a very difficult study of the whole question of the incidence of taxation. There are no simple or easy answers to this, Mr. Speaker. The answers which have been given by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) are the best which can be provided. Presumably they are not good enough for the mover of the motion; he wants answers which will suit his own purposes. I am reminded of the old story about the facts: that if they do not suit the theory then so much the worse for the facts. We have given the facts to the hon. member in the most careful, polished and complete form in which they can be presented with academic integrity, and I use that phrase to this house in its very best sense. There can be no useful purpose served

by the mover of the motion's seeking to go beyond the presentation which has been made and seeking to explore through compelling disclosure of early drafts, working papers and incomplete statements a matter as explosive, as difficult and as emotional as this one.
These are days, Mr. Speaker, when perhaps greater strains are laid on our confederate structure than have been laid for many decades. There is an onus on all of us to be responsible in our public statements and to be responsible in this house. We should not lightly without good reason question such a matter as a formal statement by the Minister of Finance disclosing the origins of taxes and the destination of expenditures by provinces, such as that prepared in the way this return has been prepared. We raise much greater questions of national unity if we seek to go beyond the best professional competence and judgment of the officials of the department who have been responsible for the preparation of the order for return and the material contained in it.
For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that we have no choice but to say that this is not the kind of motion which should be accepted by this house. It is wrong because it seeks to compel premature disclosure of information which is not complete in itself. It is wrong because it would challenge the very integrity of those in the public service who are entrusted with research and investigation operations in various government departments. It is wrong because it seeks to give a distorted and very dangerous interpretation, within the present context of our confederation, of what one area gives and receives compared to what another area gives and receives. It is wrong because it seeks in the course of a public debate to deal with matters of an intricate and technical nature involving the compilation and interpretation of statistical data which can only be collected by those, in justice to the persons concerned, who are trained to interpret and understand that data, data which should not be misused for any narrow political or partisan advantage.
For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, and for many other reasons which can be advanced, I think it would be proper for the mover of the motion to say to the house at this time that this is not the procedure for seeking such information. The procedure for seeking such information is by putting questions on the order paper. The questions which have been placed on the order paper dealing with

this matter have been answered. If there is a question concerning the nature and validity of the assumptions and the interpretation of the material, then the most satisfactory procedure is again to phrase additional questions dealing with the returns which have been filed. These questions can be stated precisely. They can be framed by the hon. member, if necessary by consulting with persons who are trained, to make sure that the proper points are raised, and the answers can be prepared and filed accordingly. This procedure is the orderly, responsible and I suggest the sensible way of dealing with this matter.
The alternative procedure would, in my submission, seek to compel the premature and I would suggest disturbing publication of incomplete, early, preliminary notes, preliminary findings and preliminary tables which are in many cases prepared by a junior officer who is assigned to the project, and subsequently reviewed by his senior in that particular section or division. Any procedure which distorts the research process by placing the civil servants involved in a position where their academic integrity and reputation would inevitably be jeopardized is one which I am sure on reflection will not commend itself to many members of this house.
I would strongly suggest to the very utmost of whatever persuasive powers I possess that the mover of the motion should withdraw it; that he should have recourse to the alternative of phrasing questions which can be put on the order paper and which can deal with any particular aspect of the problem which he feels has not properly or adequately been answered in the order for return which was tabled by the Minister of Finance in reply to the question posed by the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer). Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I would ask the mover of the motion to withdraw it. I think the reasons for withdrawing it are compelling. Failing withdrawal I believe there is no alternative but for the members of this house to say that the principle involved here in moving this motion is repugnant to us, that we cannot accept it and that in all conscience we must vote against it should it come to a vote, which I sincerely hope the mover of the motion will refrain from asking.

If in order to give us an extra amount the Minister of Finance incurs a deficit, why then include the deficit in the figures he gave us? That is not very smart.
In other words, in the $915 million which is deemed to have been given to the province of Quebec at the rate of so much per capita, they cannot say why it is such an amount. No details have been given. It is known there is one billion dollars in regard to the debt interest, but it is neither the citizens of the province of Quebec nor those of Ontario who receive the interest on the debt. The interest is paid in a proportion of between 70 and 75 per cent to foreigners: Americans, English, Belgians, Swiss, French, Italians. That money does not find its way into our province.
We are told that the $915 million going back to the province of Quebec includes a part of defence expenditures totalling $1.5 billion. But we can hardly say that when we bought Voodoos, Bomarcs and nuclear arms in the United States, weapons that will never be used again, such expenditures were made in the interest of one province only, no.
And when the amount includes a deficit, because the money must come from somewhere, and we learned a moment ago that it did come from a deficit, that deficit is not passed on to the citizens of a province. However, interest must be paid on the deficit.
Therefore, the amount should not be based on what we receive but on what we pay.
The figures submitted by the Minister of Finance are misleading.
Why could we not be told how half or nearly half the total amount is redistributed?

For instance, in the case of the Farm Credit Corporation the province of Quebec gets practically nothing. In the case of expenditures of the federal government in the field of transportation, for railway crossings or installation of traffic lights, for instance, Quebec gets 25 per cent. The same thing can be said about expenditures of the Department of Fisheries where Quebec only gets a very small percentage of the amount involved.
The estimates of the Department of Finance amount to $83 million, $48 million of which are going to the wheat board, that is to the three prairie provinces, while $10 million were spent on reforestation across the country but not a single penny in the province of Quebec.
But the Minister of Finance received reports and was faced with complications. Then the results were disastrous for his department because he noticed that there was a lack of balance in the country as a whole. At that time he made it a point to hide the true figures and statistics. He included them in a total of $915 million, saying: it is so much per capita, but there was no question of figuring out the debt in each province. It was said: it is so much per capita. That is less incriminating.
Mr. Speaker, we got only part of the report the Minister of Finance was supposed to give us. We did not get the whole thing. We feel that even if he let us have part of it, the Minister of Finance should now give us a breakdown of the $915 million remaining, which make up more than half the total.
The people of Canada must know the facts as well as the House of Commons. Nor will we be content with a partial reply; we want a full reply.
That is why we will ask a vote to be taken on that matter, and then we will see who, in this House of Commons, wants things out in broad daylight, and who, through their votes, will indicate that they prefer to hide the truth, to keep it under a bushel.

Mr. Speaker-
Getting on with the country's business.

-as the minister said, we are getting on with the country's business by establishing a number of banks. This matter is of considerable interest to me because I have been interested in the negotiations that have taken place in recent years between the banking institutions that we have, the number of banks that have been established and their relationship particularly to the small loans field. It has been of interest to me, Mr. Speaker, to learn that all the banks we now have, and they are not numerous in Canada, have been more interested in amalgamation than they have been in establishing a number of small regional banks.
I believe that this whole problem of banking should have been referred, as it is necessary by law to do every ten years, to the appropriate committee for discussion. There should have been a decision with regard to the policy to be followed under the Bank Act for the next ten years, before these bills were brought before parliament. You will recall that some of our major banks, banks which have been in operation many years, have amalgamated. The Imperial Bank of Canada, recently amalgamated with the Bank of Com-

Private Bills
merce to form the Imperial Bank of Commerce. This has been repeated by several of the other major banks. In fact there has been a tendency for banks to amalgamate and we are now faced with a new concept in the banking facilities of the nation, particularly in relation to the proposed Laurentide bank.
This is an institution which warrants a great deal of attention from members, particularly with regard to the reasons why it is proposed. It will be a rather unique bank, with a wholesale-retail operation. The bank will wholesale for its retail outlet, the Laurentide Trust and Finance Company. How will this work and how will it fit into the pattern we have established for banks in the national sphere?
This is a bank that will not need to deal in loans as do other banks, and it is interesting to note that the parent company recently bought a finance company which is in a dubious position and whose affairs are now before the courts.
We have not been able to examine fully this matter of vertical integration in the banking industry. There must be reasons why the old stalwart banks have found it necessary to amalgamate, and they have reached great size by doing so.
We have had very stable banking institutions in Canada. At times members of parliament have been distressed because of the policy taken by individual banks in relation to retail credit, but on the whole our banking institutions have been responsible, and have been subject to control, suggestion and direction by the government of the nation. Governments will continue to give such direction and for this reason it makes one wonder why we are now embarking on a new course which we have not previously allowed.
Several banks have been able to take advantage of the ceiling on small loans to charge interest rates greater than the 6 per cent which by law is allowed. They have been able to do this through such things as insurance, and devaluating the value placed on the collateral pledged with them. In many cases they have been able to boost interest rates to 12 per cent, 14 per cent and even higher; but these rates do not come within the ambit of those charged by finance companies, including the Laurentide Trust and Finance Company, because many of these charge interest rates as high as 30 and 40 per cent.
I do not believe it is in the national interest to charter a bank which will act only as a wholesale agency for its finance company. I would point out that bills to incorporate banks

are completely different from other private bills which come before parliament, such as those dealing with divorce or the building of pipe lines. I believe a committee of both houses should be made aware of policy changes with respect to the Bank Act. As we know, by law it is necessary to review it every ten years, and it is shortly due for revision. I think any decision on the chartering of new banks should await policy decision with respect to this revision.
It is also interesting that this is a Senate bill. Many editorials have appeared in newspapers questioning the impartiality of members of the other house to decide on certain banking bills, when hon. members of that house themselves in many cases are members of the boards of directors of competing banks.

I do not believe it is necessary to argue at length for this amendment. Hon. members will realize what it seeks to do. It is still my view, as it was the view of the Minister of Transport and his colleagues when they sat on this side of the house in the parliament before the last, that parliament should know if not the actual persons, at least the kind of persons being put on a commission of this kind. It is my view also that we should not leave this all to the Speaker without giving him some guidelines to give him an indication of the kind of person parliament has in mind.
My earlier amendment, which has been turned down by the committee, suggested that there be two categories and that whoever made the appointments should pick the two members, one from one category and one from the other. The committee having turned down that proposition, like the hon. member for Bow River I am offering a compromise. I suggest that we lay out at least one type of person from whom the Speaker ought to make the choice. I have in the amendment used the words "if possible", for the obvious reason that these persons are not federal employees and hence, if the Speaker is not able to get the consent of the chief electoral officer of the province or such person to take on the assignment, the Speaker will need to have the right to pick someone else in that province whom he deems to be suitable.
As was pointed out this afternoon by the Minister of Transport, the whole idea that I have put forward is based on the very successful experience we have had in the province of Manitoba, where we have the only province-wide independent, impartial commission working in this field. In that province the commission consists of the chief electoral officer, the president of the university and the chief justice of the province. It has worked very well there. I think it would be good for us to suggest to the Speaker that if he is going to make these appointments parliament would like something along that line. Mr. Chairman, so far as I myself am concerned I think it would make relatively little difference to the actual distribution which would take place whether the tolerance was 20 per cent or 25 per cent. Certainly I would not be prepared to support any figure higher than 25 per cent. I think we should face the fact, regardless of what is the actual tolerance, that if these commissions do their job conscientiously, they will try as far as possible to hew to the line. A tolerance is a tolerance. It is not meant to be a licence to go as far as possible away from what parliament wants. It is to meet hard situations that may arise. Without hard situations it could be done not by commissions at all but by I.B.M. machines, computers or something of that sort. That would be the fairest way of all to have redistribution, except that it would be utterly inhuman and would produce ridiculous results. It is to meet these human situations that there is a tolerance at all and that we depart from the strict rule of representation by population.
I do not think there is anyone in the committee who would argue that there should
[The Chairman.]

not be some tolerance; there is in every country where this kind of redistribution exists. It varies from one country to another, and the tendency over the years has been to make the figure smaller. But speaking for myself I would not in the least object if the general view was that it should remain at 20 per cent or if the general view was that it should be 25 per cent. As far as I am concerned I am quite prepared to support either position.
I think the best way of deciding this question is this. If someone wants to vary it he could move-I do not mind doing it myself and am quite prepared to do so if that is the general feeling-that the tolerance be 25 per cent. Let us think of some of the provinces which have a special tolerance. For example, the maritimes cannot have less members-and I am sure everyone agrees- than the number of senators from that area. There has been a lot of misunderstanding about the tolerance figure. If there is a tolerance of 10 per cent it does not mean that you would have 70,000 people plus 10 per cent. If the tolerance is 20 per cent it does not mean you would have 70,000 people plus 20 per cent. If you had a tolerance of 25 per cent it does not mean you would have 70,000 people in each constituency plus 25 per cent. All constituencies should consist of 70,000 people. It might be 72,000 now because the population of Canada has gone up since the last census. The figure could be zero; it could be 1 per cent. But a percentage is called for in the bill. The division of the province into electoral districts and the description of the boundaries thereof shall proceed on the basis that the population of each electoral district in the province as a result thereof shall correspond as nearly as may be to the electoral quota for the province-
I had the good fortune of seeing the map prepared by the office of the chief electoral officer. In our area of northwestern Quebec, that is in the counties of Chapleau and Vil-leneuve-and I am not only concerned about my own riding here-emphasis has been laid on clause 13 (b) which reads as follows:
(b) The commission may be depart from the strict application of rule (a) in any case where
(i) special geographic considerations-

We explained that Chapleau county went up to Janies Bay and that in view of geographic considerations, we should divide the two counties, or even the three counties of Pontiac-Temiscamingue, Villeneuve and Chapleau, leaving Noranda in Villeneuve county, Rouyn in Pontiac-Temiscamingue county, adding Villeneuve to Amos, St. Marc de Figurie and Senneterre, and then leave in Chapleau county the northern part of the province where there are hardly any inhabitants except Indians, perhaps 1,500 to
2.000	at the most, which would not change much in the next ten years.
At present, changes are made in the ridings because it is said that population is no longer important and that geography is the basis of everything.
Then, I found that the proposed solution was perfectly unreasonable, namely to add to the Villeneuve riding the towns of Amos, St. Marc, Senneterre, Barraute, Belcourt, and make a Chapleau riding from the Ontario boundary, that is from La Reine, La Sarre, Malartic, Taschereau, then, turning above Amos, and following the railway line to Parent, and then going north to Chibougamau.
Those are geographic considerations where there is no population, where the towns and villages I just mentioned are taken away from Chapleau.
We cannot admit that. The Pontiac-Temiscamingue riding is all right as it is, the Villeneuve riding is all right as it is and the Chapleau riding is also well as it is, even if the territory of Chapleau is twice as large as that of Villeneuve and Pontiac-Temiscamingue, because there is no population. 200.000	voters, while a small riding, has only
25.000	or 30,000. Then, changes must be made; a redistribution is necessary, but not in rural ridings such as ours in the northern area.
