It is my understanding that those of us who represent sparsely settled regions will stand to gain very much by the fact the tolerance is set at 25 per cent, and that this 25 per cent is almost certain to be operating as a minus factor rather than a plus factor. Whether it does or not, great changes are certain in the hinterland areas, much more so than almost any other part of the country including the large cities.
As I interpret this, it is actually to my advantage or to the advantage of the electors in my area if I support the 25 per cent tolerance rather than the 20 per cent. However, I intend to vote against the amendment. I would put it to the members in the house, particularly those who represent cities that, although the effect may be small, if you go along with the 25 per cent tolerance you just get that much farther away from the one man, one vote and one representative concept. I myself would support, even though again it is going to be more difficult to change some of these hinterland areas, a tolerance of 10 per cent. I just wanted to express the fact that I am going to vote against the amendment, and I know some of my colleagues will. I believe one or two of them would be prepared to have an even larger tolerance.

reason that redistribution commissioners, in effect, will have an office going all the time. We know that office is already conscious of some of the transitions that are taking place. We would hope, since we are likely to have two redistributions within much less than a decade, that there will be some experienced personnel. For that reason, I think it would be quite valuable to have this rate of growth concept embodied in the provision.
One of the things that has bothered me about the approach of the minister tonight as I have understood it, not least about the general line that is going around about this question of tolerance, is the line that it really does not matter that much whether the tolerance is set at 35 per cent or 25 per cent; that it is at the discretion of the commissioner. I asked him today whether there were any changes in orders in council in reference to the zoning of parks and a building permit. There are various areas zoned in the townsite of Banff for business, and certain sections are zoned as residential areas. I suggest to the minister that the Bow River project, which is going to be a three-storey hotel with a cocktail lounge, is being built in the best residential part of Banff townsite and in an area which has that beauty that makes building on it contrary to the terms and conditions of the National Parks Act. But the worst thing of all is that the minister said today these orders in council were not rescinded; they were only rescinded in regard to this particular project. I want to read to the minister something for which he has perhaps a great deal of respect, namely the words of Mackenzie King, when it comes to passing orders in council, particularly in secret. That is why I wanted them filed in the house. We noticed that the minister was most reluctant today to answer the questions. This is what Mackenzie King said in reference to these secret orders in council. This was the statement quoted by Senator Power who was then a member of parliament in this House of Commons. He was dealing with the law and he said, in brief, that the law should be known to every Canadian. This is what Mackenzie King said:
Now let us come to another point, which I wish particularly to stress. I refer to the right set out in Magna Carta that no man shall be dispossessed of his rights without the lawful Judgment of his peers under the law of the land; not the law as made by the governor in council, not the law as made by some unnamed and as yet unexisting
10040	HOUSE OF
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion body, but the law of the land as known to everyone. It is an essential principle of liberty and freedom that the law of the land should be known, that it should be so known that every man as he runs may read. The law should not be something which is to make its appearance in the Canada Gazette after some board or governor in council, not parliament, has passed a regulation; it is something that should appear in the statutes of the country.
In brief, Mr. Speaker, we have certain orders in council known to the council of Banff, an elected body, and the minister in order to give-and I suggest to him this is suspicious-certain people the right to build certain things in Banff, amended those laws unknown to parliament, unknown to the people of Canada and unknown to Banff, and refused today to table them until pressed by myself, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefen-baker) and the former minister. I wish I had time in the seven minutes at my disposal, but I have not, to read from the minutes what the minister said at his meeting with the council of Banff. I have a copy of the minutes, which give word for word what took place between himself and the elected body of Banff. He said to that body, in brief, in Calgary recently, "You apologize to the Prime Minister and myself, because you asked for my resignation from the Prime Minister. If you don't apologize, I won't even listen to you. You mean nothing to me", I am going to read what he said to these people. This is what he said as reported at page 8 of these minutes, taken right at the meeting. I would say it was the most disgraceful performance of any minister in this country, to speak to an elected body in the manner in which he spoke to them. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on orders of the day this afternoon I asked the Prime Minister whether he could disclose the terms of his answer to those who saw the government two weeks ago concerning the need for an increase in the pensions of superannuated civil servants. The Prime Minister indicated briefly what those terms were, and press reports have spelled them out in more detail and indicate in fact that the government's answer to this very urgent appeal was no.
Mr. Speaker, I express on behalf of superannuated civil servants and widows of superannuated civil servants great disappointment that the government has again given this kind of an answer. Earlier during this session representations were made to the government. They were dealt with by the Minister of Finance, and after a period of time he gave a negative answer. As the weeks and months of this session have passed, further representations have been made. Finally two weeks ago Tuesday, I believe, representatives of two or three bodies speaking for superannuated civil servants met with the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance, and I believe one or two other ministers, and
10042	HOUSE OF
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion presented their case. They were assured that their case would be given consideration. Now again they have been told that this government can do nothing for them.
The arguments which are given are not new, and I suggest that they are no more valid today than they were when given on past occasions. The principal argument that the government seems to use again and again is that superannuated civil servants should not expect anything better than pensioned employees of other employers in the country. Surely if that argument carries any weight, then no one in the government service can expect better salaries or conditions than those found elsewhere in the country. Surely this argument is full of holes, and what the government ought to be doing is to be leading rather than dragging behind other employers.
The suggestion that other employers do not do this is also made from time to time. I find that an increasing number of employers, particularly municipal organizations, some of the provinces, as well as employers in other countries are recognizing that retired employees have a right to share in the increased productivity of the society or nation of which they have been a part. I suggest that this principle was in fact accepted by parliament in 1959 when it passed the Public Service Pension Adjustment Act. This of course was when a Conservative government was in power but the Liberals of that day did not oppose the measure. In other words, any suggestion that it is a sin or a crime to raise the pensions of former government employees was surely set aside by the action that parliament took on that occasion.
One of the other suggestions made by the Prime Minister, according to press reports, is that the government is doing things for older people generally and that superannuated civil servants must be satisfied to share in these general improvements. Apparently one of the improvements cited is that the old age security pension is going to have built into it a cost of living bonus. We now know what that means. It means that in 1968, if superannuated civil servants drawing the old age security pension are still alive, they stand a chance of getting an increase in their old age security pension of 75 cents a month or if the cost of living has gone up high enough they will get $1.50 a month but no more. When we talk about 1968 in relation to old people obviously many of them will be dead before that time comes.


I submit that the government is being callous and unfair to these former employees and that it is being unfair to the desire of Canadians as a whole to be decent to our employees. I submit that the government is completely wrong in its failure to give a lead of any kind. This very day the Prime Minister, in response to a question from the Leader of the Opposition with regard to veterans pensions, admitted that perhaps with respect to veterans pensions the time had come for a cyclical review of these pensions every two years. Indeed, even the cost of living bonus in the Canada pension plan and in the Old Age Security Act is an admission there is a case for these amounts to be reviewed and increased after pensions have been put in payment.
I submit that on all counts the government is being most unfair to its former employees, the superannuated civil servants, retired members of the services, of the mounted police and others, in continually saying no to these faithful former servants. This is supposed to be a question, Mr. Speaker, and obviously I have been making a statement expressing my disappointment at the announcement made by the Prime Minister today on orders of the day. I close with a question. What has the government got to say to give some hope, some encouragement, to these former employees?

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre in expressing himself suggested that the government was callous in its attitude toward this question. His criticism affords me the opportunity to remind him that no one has a more sincere regard and deeper concern for pensioners and other retired people in this country than the Prime Minister, and as head of the government he has translated that concern into constructive action on more than one occasion.
The Prime Minister, with real regret, was impelled to make the decision in regard to this matter which he announced to the house. We transmitted that decision in the form of a letter to Mr. Fred W. Whitehouse, national secretary-treasurer of the federal superannuates national association, in a letter similar in substance to Mr. F. T. Gough, national secretary-treasurer of the civil service association of Canada and in another letter to Mr. J. G. Dumouchel, first vice-president of the civil service federation of Canada. My colleagues and I have studied the brief which you left with me on October 27 when we had a discussion concerning your proposal to adjust the pensions paid to superannuated civil servants.

maintopic: GRAIN-PRINCE RUPERT, B.C.-INCREASE IN ELEVATOR CAPACITY
GRAIN-PRINCE RUPERT, B.C.-INCREASE IN ELEVATOR CAPACITY
speechtext:
I raised by way of question today, and have done so on many other days in the past, the subject of the grain elevator in the city of Prince Rupert, a terminal point on the Canadian National Railway. On each of the many occasions upon which I have asked the minister about prospects for doubling the capacity of that elevator he has said, either directly or in effect, that the matter is under consideration.
The elevator at Prince Rupert, by the admission of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) himself, is one of the most efficiently operated terminal elevators in Canada. It has a working capacity of about one million bushels. Grain handling ships today are of a size now that they can carry upwards from three quarters of a million bushels in one cargo. This leaves the elevator in a position of being unable to load more than one ship at a time. It would have to wait, after one ship is loaded, for an influx of grain by rail, then have the grain cleaned, processed and stored until the approximately three quarters of a million bushels capacity was reached again, which would be sufficient for another ship of similar size.
In recent years we have seen tremendously large sales of grain to other countries, notably to China and the Soviet union, which have resulted in the west coast ports being used to the maximum. They have also resulted in the city of Vancouver, as it were, getting the gravy. A further result was an announcement just a few months ago of a large increase in the capacity of one of the elevators in Vancouver, and as a consequence the city of Prince Rupert and the operation of the grain elevator there are being pushed more and more into the background.
Nearly every argument or reason that one can think of is in favour of doubling the

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion capacity of the elevator there. Incidentally, it was built with this thought in mind in 1926, at a cost-and I am guessing-of between $1J million and $2 million, so that its capacity could be doubled. On March 31 of this year we had a debate in this chamber about the Prince Rupert elevator and the minister answered me as follows:
I am quite sympathetic to what the hon. member has said, and I am sorry that I cannot say tonight some of the things I should like to say. But I can say this, that all of the storage facilities which are controlled by the Canadian government in one way or another have been carefully discussed, and I hope in the not too distant future that we will be able to present something to the hon. member which will be satisfactory in so far as the Prince Rupert terminal is concerned.
That was at the end of March and now it is pretty near the end of the year.
Mr. Speaker, the people in Rupert have been waiting and living in hope since that day, and even before that day. Each time we pose the question to the minister the only answer we get is the same as we got today, namely that it is under consideration. It has even got to the point where the minister says this laughingly, as if it were a joke. But it is not a joke; it is a very serious matter.
Maybe it was appropriate that the minister made those comments on March 31, the eve of April Fool's day. Perhaps he had in mind perpetrating an April Fool's joke on the people of Rupert. I hope not, and I hope that he will soon finish his consideration. Surely it does not take months and months of dragged out consideration to come to a conclusion. I ask him to tell the people in Rupert whether the government is going to double the elevator capacity or not? This is the simple answer the people want. They think this consideration has gone on far too

long. It is long past the time for action. They would like to see this take place, and so would I.

speechtext:
I also want to assure him that the Minister of Agriculture is interested in every aspect of agriculture, and not the least of his interest is in the provision of proper facilities for the handling of grain, including the terminal elevator at Prince Rupert.
The minister of course is justified in this interest in view of the fact that in 1963 we harvested the largest crop of wheat and grain in our history, amounting to some 725 million bushels, and of this total some 632 million bushels were sold for export. When you add to that the amount of grain used domestically, which amounted to another 155 million bushels, this indicates our total output for that year was more than the total amount harvested, which of course means we have eaten into our reserves.
The hon. member for Skeena will realize that by asking this type of question he is inquiring into what government policy might be, and I have no alternative but to reply that this matter has been given very thorough consideration and is being considered constantly, and when an announcement is possible it will be made by the minister in the house.

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-REPLY OF PRIME MINISTER TO FEDERAL SUPERANNUATES NATIONAL ASSOCIATION

speechtext:
Ottawa, November 10, 1964.
Mr. Fred W. Whitehouse,
National Secretary-Treasurer,
Federal Superannuates National Association,
2696 MacDonald Drive,
Victoria, B.C.
Dear Mr. Whitehouse:
My colleagues and I have studied the brief which you left with me on October 27 when we had a discussion concerning your proposal to adjust the pensions paid to superannuated civil servants.
After reviewing the principles involved in your proposal as well as the facts which you have cited, we have come to the conclusion that any steps which the government should propose to parliament to alleviate difficulties faced by retired persons should be general in character and not confined to former employees of the government of Canada. I am sure that your association will recognize on reflection that there have been a number of general actions taken which have benefitted members of your association as well as other retired people in Canada; the main ones, of course, have been the increases in the old age security pensions. Already those over 70 will have received benefits increased by $240 per year per pensioner over the level that pertained at the time the Public Service Pension Adjustment Act was passed in 1958. In addition, there have been corresponding increases in old age assistance for those who require it between the ages of 65 and 70, as well as other measures taken by the provinces to meet the situation of those in need. In addition to this, hospital insurance has become available to retired persons on a national basis since that time. Since retired people constitute a high-cost group under such insurance, the establishment of hospital insurance programs is of quite substantial help to them.
Under the provisions of the Canada pension plan bill which has just been made public the amount of the old age security pension available to all Canadians meeting the residence qualifications will be adjusted to take into account changes in the cost of living. Consequently, when this bill is enacted by parliament members of your association will be able to rely upon the real value of their old age security pension being maintained.
The government believes that it would be unfair to the great majority of retired Canadians who have not worked for the government to make special provision to protect the former employees of the government of Canada itself against increases in living costs. Pensions paid to former government employees under the Superannuation Act or under other similar acts must be looked upon basically as part of the remuneration received by these employees for the services they rendered when they were employed. They are not payments based upon need, nor should they be regarded as payments that are subject to increase on compassionate grounds. To make them such would be to favour this minority of retired people by comparison with the majority of other retired Canadians who cannot expect such treatment either from the government as such or from employers for whom they had worked in the past. In this sense, to accede to the requests of your association would constitute a form of discrimination against the majority.
It is with real regret that I send you a decision which I know will be disappointing to you and to the members of your association, but I feel it would be unfair to them to leave the situation uncertain once the government had reviewed the principles involved in your proposal and come to the reluctant conclusion that it could not accept them.
Yours sincerely,
L. B. Pearson.
Friday, November 13, 1964
